prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Make the diagnosis of migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) on clinical grounds: no red flag is present, so no neuroimaging is needed.

Start sumatriptan 50-100 mg at headache onset (not during the aura), which may be combined with ibuprofen 400 mg or naproxen 500 mg, with an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg) for nausea and vomiting; nasal or subcutaneous sumatriptan if vomiting prevents oral dosing.
No preventive treatment now: about one severe headache day a month is below the AHS 2021 threshold; keep a headache diary and reassess if disabling headache days increase or acute treatment fails.
Advise limiting acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month for triptans and fewer than 15 days for simple analgesics to avoid medication-overuse headache.

Advise that combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring) is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; if contraception or treatment for dysmenorrhoea is wanted, offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD (the levonorgestrel IUS also treats dysmenorrhoea).

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve it for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT or for meningitis, neither of which is present here.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; it has a role only when cardioembolic stroke is in question.
OCT is not part of the migraine work-up; it is reserved for optic neuropathy or chiasmal disease, which are not in question here.

differential.diagnosis: Migraine without aura with visual symptoms
differential.key_features: Stereotyped fortification spectra expanding over 20-30 min before every headache are a visual aura, not the non-specific visual blurring that can accompany migraine without aura.

differential.diagnosis: Focal occipital seizure with visual phenomena
differential.key_features: Visual seizures are brief (<2 min), stereotyped colored circles; 20-30 min spread is too slow for ictal propagation; no impaired awareness
5-year recurrent identical pattern, young patient, no vascular risk factors; gradual aura march is incompatible with abrupt TIA onset
No haemorrhage, no thunderclap onset, no deficit between attacks, and aura and headache alternate sides (a side-locked aura would raise an occipital AVM and justify MRI).

key_clinical_evidence: ICHD-3 1.2.1 is a clinical diagnosis: no neuroimaging or laboratory test confirms migraine with aura when the criteria are met
No red flag: onset at 23, normal examination, gradual aura, aura side alternates; routine brain MRI is not indicated [AHS_neuroimaging_2020]
About one severe headache day a month is below the AHS 2021 threshold for preventive treatment; acute treatment is a triptan at headache onset with an NSAID and antiemetic
Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura

findings.result: Recurrent stereotyped attacks for 5 years; frequency rose from about every 6 weeks to almost monthly over the past year.
Visual only: scintillating crescent expanding into a zigzag fortification arc in the peripheral field of one side, right more often than left. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Gradual expansion over 20-30 min, then fades; fully reversible.

Throbbing headache, 8/10, after the aura resolves, usually contralateral to the aura, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, vomiting in about half; lasts 6-12 h. About 1 headache day a month, severely disabling.
Menstruation, sleep deprivation, missed meals. Ibuprofen 400 mg partly effective; triptan-naive.
Headache-free. Normal cranial nerves, visual fields by confrontation and fundi (no papilloedema); normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. BP 116/72 mmHg.

Systemic symptoms or fever: absent. Neoplasia history: absent. Neurological deficit between attacks: absent. Sudden onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 23). Pattern change: frequency increase only, aura and headache character unchanged. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Pregnancy: not pregnant. Aura always on the same side: absent (alternates). No red flag present.

clinical_assessment.impression: Recurrent fully reversible visual aura with gradual spread over 20-30 min, followed by headache: meets ICHD-3 1.2.1.1 typical aura with headache (criterion C 5 of 6). No red flag; aura side alternates; normal examination.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 28-year-old woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation and management of recurrent headaches with visual symptoms that she has experienced for the past 5 years, now almost once a month. Each episode begins with a shimmering, crescent-shaped visual disturbance in the periphery of one visual field (more often the right, sometimes the left) that gradually expands into a flickering zigzag arc (fortification spectra) over 20-30 minutes, then fades. During this visual aura she cannot read effectively and describes the phenomenon as like 'looking through a kaleidoscope.' After the visual aura resolves, she develops a severe one-sided throbbing headache (8/10 intensity), usually on the side opposite the visual disturbance, with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia lasting 6-12 hours. Vomiting occurs in approximately half of episodes. She takes ibuprofen 400 mg which only partially helps. She has not tried triptans. She denies any limb weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, or loss of consciousness associated with the episodes. Between attacks she is entirely normal.

She has a maternal aunt with similar migraines. She reports that episodes are triggered by menstruation, sleep deprivation, and skipping meals. Oral contraceptive pills were prescribed by her GP 2 years ago for dysmenorrhea but she stopped them after 6 months because she felt they increased headache frequency. She has no history of stroke, hypertension, diabetes, or cardiac disease. She is a graphic designer, non-smoker, moderate caffeine use. The frequency of attacks has increased from one every 6 weeks to almost monthly over the past year, prompting this referral.
